title: Polish-Lithuania Kingdom
capsule: The Jagiellonian dynasty was a Lithuanian-Polish ruling house descended from Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania, who converted to Christianity and was crowned King of Poland as Władysław II Jagiełło in 1386 following the Union of Krewo (1385), creating a dynastic link between the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Kingdom of Poland. At its apex the dynasty simultaneously ruled Poland, Lithuania, Bohemia, and Hungary, making it the dominant royal house of east-central Europe; the Battle of Grunwald (1410), where Władysław II defeated the Teutonic Knights, secured Polish-Lithuanian hegemony in the Baltic region. The male Jagiellonian line ended with the death of Sigismund II Augustus in 1572, after which Poland-Lithuania elected its kings, though the dataset's span to 1571 reflects the last full decade before this dynastic transition.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Jagiellonian territorial extent is well attested from royal charters, diet records, and ecclesiastical sources for Poland and Lithuania; Bohemian and Hungarian holdings are documented but the dataset geometry for the composite state carries moderate spatial uncertainty at frontiers.
